::: {.why}
Half the strategies in this year are long-short, and the short leg carries a financing cost, a recall risk and a dividend obligation that no price series will ever show you.
:::

## What you should be able to do tonight

- Walk through a short sale in the order the steps happen: locate, borrow, sell, mark, return.
- State what you owe when the stock you are short pays a dividend, and what a recall forces you to do at the worst possible moment.

## Tasks <span class='task-total'>60 min</span>

::: {.task-list}
::: {.task}
<input type="checkbox" class="task-check"> [25 min]{.task-min} Read the Efficiently Inefficient introduction chapter section on short selling and the limits of arbitrage. Pedersen's account of why an arbitrage can be right and still bankrupt you is the one to have in your head from now on.
:::
::: {.task}
<input type="checkbox" class="task-check"> [20 min]{.task-min} Write the short-sale sequence into the glossary with the cash flows attached: what you receive, what you pay in borrow, what you owe on the dividend, and what the rebate on your short proceeds is worth at current short rates. Use the two borrow numbers you looked up last night.
:::
::: {.task}
<input type="checkbox" class="task-check"> [15 min]{.task-min} Compute the drag: a market-neutral strategy holds 100 percent long and 100 percent short. At a 40-basis-point general collateral borrow fee, what does the short leg cost per year, in basis points of gross exposure? Now redo it at 8 percent for a hard-to-borrow name.
:::
:::

::: {.deliverable}
The short-sale glossary entry with every cash flow named, plus the two borrow-cost calculations in basis points a year.
:::

## Checkpoint

::: {.checkpoint}
Your short position is recalled on the day the stock gaps up 20 percent. Describe what you have to do and what it costs you.
:::
